deed: אברהם בר חייא כתב את חיבור המשיחה והתשבורת — ואירופה למדה ממנו לפתור משוואות ריבועיות
title: Abraham bar Hiyya wrote a book on measurement in Hebrew, and Europe learned from it to solve quadratic equations

trailer.text: Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi was a Jewish mathematician, astronomer and philosopher who lived and worked in Spain. In Latin he is known as Savasorda.

He wrote Hibbur ha-Meshihah ve-ha-Tishboret in Hebrew; according to Curtze, the original introduction, which the Latin translator omitted, is reported to have addressed the Jews of France, and in it he said that he had written the work for their use ‹c50›.
The book was translated into Latin by Plato of Tivoli as Liber embadorum.
According to MacTutor, it is the first text in Europe to give a complete solution of the general quadratic equation.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography (DSB), Fibonacci was also influenced by him.

glance.label: Who
glance.value: Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi (Savasorda), a Spanish Jewish mathematician and astronomer

glance.label: When
glance.value: According to an article from the University of Haifa, 'Ḥibbur ha-Meshiḥah ve-ha-Tishboret' was published in 1116.

glance.label: In Latin
glance.value: Liber embadorum, translated by Plato of Tivoli

glance.label: Influence
glance.value: Fibonacci and his book Practica geometriae

paragraphs.text: According to the DSB, Savasorda spent most of his life in Barcelona, an area of Arab and Christian learning.
According to Steinschneider, as quoted by Curtze, he lived at the end of the 11th century and the beginning of the 12th century.
According to the Spanish Biographical Dictionary, he held a high public office at the court of the Counts of Barcelona.
In the Hebrew of his time "Ha-Nasi" meant "the leader".
According to MacTutor, the Latin name Savasorda also comes from his "job description", and according to the University of Haifa article it indicates a high public and legal office.
According to Curtze, he was granted the honorary title of head of the guard, and his translator Plato of Tivoli distorted it into Savasorda.
According to Curtze, he stayed in Provence and southern France only temporarily.
According to the Spanish dictionary, he apparently helped the Counts of Barcelona divide territories, as seems to follow from his treatise on surveying.

According to the Spanish dictionary, Bar Hiyya alluded in one of his works, without the dictionary specifying which, to his work as a translator from Arabic into Hebrew, and wrote that there is no Hebrew book in all the land of France dealing with these sciences, and therefore he translated from Arabic books.

According to Curtze, summarizing Steinschneider, the translator omitted the original introduction; reportedly, it addressed the Jews of France and accused them of not properly knowing the rules of geometry and therefore making incorrect calculations.
According to the DSB, he deplored the lack of knowledge of Arab science and the Arabic language among the people of Provence.
According to Springer, in response to requests from Jews in Provence, Bar Hiyya produced a series of Hebrew texts in astronomy and mathematics.
According to Curtze, the introduction to the work, which the translator omitted, says that Bar Hiyya wrote the work for the use of the Jews of France.

stations.title: Inside the book: squares, fields and the circle

paragraphs.text: According to the University of Haifa article, the book is divided into four parts.
The first part contains definitions of basic concepts in geometry and arithmetic, and main theorems.
The third part deals with the division of areas, and the fourth with the calculation of volumes.
According to Curtze, the third chapter deals with the division of fields for the purposes of Arab inheritance law.
According to Curtze, in the treatise Savasorda solves problems on the area and the sum of the sides of a square or rectangle, and these are solutions of equations of the second degree.
According to Curtze, he knows that the third equation has two solutions, and proves all the cases geometrically from Book II of Euclid.
According to Curtze, he assumes that the reader already knows how to extract a square root.
According to the Haifa article, he accepted only the positive value as a solution, because in his time negative numbers had no meaning.
According to the Haifa article, he described formulas and diagrams using verbal explanations only, clearly and precisely.
According to the article, he used the numerical values of the Hebrew letters to denote numbers.
According to the article, to calculate the area of a circle he divided the circle into thin strips, straightened them and laid them one on top of another until he obtained a triangle.
According to the article, he wrote that the area of the circle is half the diameter multiplied by half the circumference.
According to the DSB, Savasorda's Hebrew treatise on practical geometry was translated into Latin by Plato of Tivoli, as Liber embadorum.
According to Curtze, Plato of Tivoli served Savasorda as an interpreter.
According to the DSB, Plato was the first to publish Ptolemy in Latin.

According to the Bar Ḥiyya entry in the DSB, Savasorda wrote his works in Hebrew but helped translate three works into Latin, and he may have worked with Plato of Tivoli on further translations; according to the Plato entry in the DSB, Plato's name appears as an editor of translations made in collaboration with Bar Ḥiyya, but in the manuscripts the translations are attributed to Plato with or without Bar Ḥiyya's name.
According to the DSB, in 1145, the year the treatise was translated, al-Khwarizmi's algebra was also translated, by Robert of Chester.
According to MacTutor, Bar Hiyya's treatise was thus rapidly joined by a second text with a complete solution of the quadratic equation.
Curtze published the Latin translation on the basis of two manuscripts of the National Library in Paris.
Curtze rejects the claim that Plato's translation is flawed, and according to him there is hardly an error in its proofs.
According to MacTutor, the treatise is the earliest Arab algebra written in Europe, and it contains a complete solution of the general quadratic equation.
According to the DSB, it is the earliest exposition of Arab algebra written in Europe, and it contains the first complete solution in Europe of the quadratic equation.
According to the DSB, the translation was the first work to introduce the solutions of quadratic equations into the Latin study of mathematics.
According to the Spanish dictionary, it has been said of the treatise that it enabled Europe to learn geometry and trigonometry.

According to the Haifa article, it is the first book in the Western world to contain knowledge of trigonometry and of the Arab theory of measurement, and for hundreds of years it served as a textbook for land surveyors.
According to Curtze, the oldest Latin table of chords is found in Savasorda.
According to the DSB, Savasorda made an innovation when he included the division of geometric figures in a practical treatise.
According to the DSB, Fibonacci was influenced by him and devoted an entire section of his book Practica geometriae to the division of figures.
According to Curtze, Fibonacci took Savasorda's treatise as a model for writing the Practica Geometriae.
According to the Haifa article, many mathematicians, among them Fibonacci, were deeply influenced by the book.
According to the Haifa article, the book's originality lies in its being the first written in Hebrew that deals with mathematics and astronomy.
According to Springer, Bar Hiyya is credited with writing the first works in Hebrew on astronomy and mathematics.
According to the Haifa article, he coined not only individual words but entire systems of scientific words and terms in Hebrew.
The Haifa article quotes Gad Ben-Ami Sarfatti, according to whom Bar Hiyya was the first to systematically expand the boundaries of the Hebrew language and give it a scientific terminology.
According to MacTutor, bar Hiyya's Yesod ha-Tevunah u-Migdal ha-Emunah is an encyclopaedia of mathematics, astronomy, optics and music, and the first encyclopaedia in Hebrew.
According to MacTutor, Sefer ha-Ibbur, written in 1122–1123, is the first Hebrew work devoted entirely to the study of the calendar.
According to MacTutor, his work, together with that of Ibn Ezra, marks the beginning of Hebrew scholarly study of mathematics.

According to MacTutor, his work appears to have stimulated an interest in Arabic mathematics, and he may be important precisely because he produced a cross-fertilisation of ideas between different cultures.
According to the Spanish dictionary, he was among the principal intermediaries between the science that had developed in the Arab world and Christian Europe.
According to the University of Haifa article, Bar Hiyya was inconsistent with certain arithmetic terms, and used different words for a single mathematical concept.
According to the article, the definition of the diameter of the circle lacks the necessary statement that it passes through the center.

disagreements.question: When was the Latin translation completed?

versions.says: Curtze: according to the manuscripts, the translation was completed on 30 June 1116
DSB (Plato of Tivoli entry): the translation was made in 1145, and the Hegira year in the manuscripts is wrong (510/1116 instead of 540/1145)
The Spanish dictionary and the University of Haifa article: the translation was made in 1145

disagreements.question: When did Abraham bar Hiyya die?

versions.says: The Spanish dictionary: there is debate among specialists, and the date 1136 has traditionally been accepted
The University of Haifa article: according to conjectures he lived between 1065 and 1136, but some hold that he was still alive in 1145

disagreements.question: Did Bar Hiyya translate together with Plato of Tivoli?

versions.says: DSB: He helped translate three works into Latin, and he may have worked with Plato on further translations; the translations are attributed to Plato with or without Bar Ḥiyya's name.
The Spanish dictionary: there is serious doubt about this, because there were several Jewish translators named Abraham in the 12th century

disagreements.question: Were Bar Ḥiyya's works the first mathematical works in Hebrew?

versions.says: Springer's Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Langermann): Bar Ḥiyya is credited with writing the first works in Hebrew on astronomy and mathematics
DSB: The earliest known Hebrew geometrical work is the Mishnat ha-Middot (c. 150 CE)

unknowns.text: There is no certain date for Bar Hiyya's death
It is not known for certain whether Bar Hiyya himself translated together with Plato of Tivoli
It is unclear whether he helped the Counts of Barcelona divide territories; the Spanish dictionary writes "apparently"

claims.text: לפי מילון הביוגרפיה המדעית, זו ההצגה המוקדמת ביותר של האלגברה הערבית שנכתבה באירופה והיא כוללת את הפתרון השלם הראשון באירופה של המשוואה הריבועית.
claims.quote: It is the earliest exposition of Arab algebra written in Europe, and it contains the first complete solution in Europe of the quadratic equation

claims.text: לפי DSB, התרגום היה החיבור הראשון שהכניס ללימוד המתמטיקה הלטיני את הפתרונות של משוואות ריבועיות.
claims.quote: In particular it was the first work to introduce into the Latin study of mathematics the solutions of quadratic equations

claims.text: לפי המילון הספרדי, נאמר על החיבור שבזכותו למדה אירופה גיאומטריה וטריגונומטריה.
claims.quote: y del que se ha dicho que sirvió para que Europa aprendiera geometría y trigonometría

claims.text: לפי המאמר מחיפה, הספר הוא הראשון בעולם המערבי שהכיל ידיעות על טריגונומטריה ועל תורת המדידות הערבית.
claims.quote: הספר מכיל הדרכה במדידות ולמעשה הוא הספר הראשון בעולם המערבי שמכיל ידיעות על הטריגונומטריה ועל תורת המדידות שהייתה ידועה לערבים .

claims.text: לפי המאמר מאוניברסיטת חיפה, הספר תורגם ללטינית ב-1145 בידי פלאטו מטיבולי ושימש מאות שנים ספר לימוד למודדי קרקעות.
claims.quote: הספר תורגם ללטינית בשנת 1145 על- ידי פלאטו מטיבולי ושימש במשך מאות שנים ספר לימוד למודדי קרקעות .

claims.text: לפי קורצה, אצל סבסורדה נמצאת טבלת המיתרים הלטינית העתיקה ביותר, כפי שהוכיח קורצה במקום אחר.
claims.quote: Dass aber bei Savasorda hier die älteste Sehnentafel in lateinischer Sprache vorhanden ist, habe ich schon in der BihliotJieca Mathematica lg, S. 330 nachgewiesen.

claims.quote: Savasorda made a novel contribution when he included the division of geometric figures in a practical treatise.

claims.quote: Bar Ḥiyya is credited with writing the first works in Hebrew on astronomy and mathematics.

claims.text: לפי המאמר מחיפה, בר חייא חידש לא רק מילים בודדות אלא מערכות שלמות של מילים ומונחים מדעיים בעברית.
claims.quote: הוא חידש לא רק מילים בודדות , אלא מערכות שלמות של מילים ושל מונחים מדעיים

claims.text: המאמר מחיפה מצטט את גד בן-עמי צרפתי, שלפיו בר חייא היה הראשון שהרחיב באופן שיטתי את גבולות הלשון העברית והנחיל לה מינוח מדעי.
claims.quote: הוא האומן הראשון אשר הרחיב בשיטתיות את גבולות הלשון העברית , והנחיל לה מינוח מדעי

claims.text: לפי MacTutor, 'יסוד התבונה ומגדל האמונה' של בר חייא הוא אנציקלופדיה של מתמטיקה, אסטרונומיה, אופטיקה ומוזיקה, והאנציקלופדיה הראשונה בעברית.
claims.quote: This work is an encyclopaedia of mathematics, astronomy, optics and music. It is the first encyclopaedia in the Hebrew language.

claims.text: ספר העיבור, שנכתב ב-1122, הוא לפי MacTutor החיבור העברי הראשון שהוקדש כולו ללוח השנה.
claims.quote: is the first Hebrew work devoted exclusively to a study of the calendar.

claims.text: לפי MacTutor, עבודתו יחד עם זו של אבן עזרא מסמנת את תחילת המחקר המתמטי העברי המלומד.
claims.quote: marks the beginning of Hebrew scholarly study of mathematics

claims.quote: it appears to have stimulated an interest in Arabic mathematics and, together with the work of

claims.quote: It may indeed be for just that reason that he is important since he produced a cross-fertilisation of ideas between these cultures.

claims.text: לפי המילון הספרדי, בר חייא היה בין המתווכים העיקריים בין המדע שהתפתח בעולם הערבי לבין אירופה הנוצרית.
claims.quote: Fue así uno de los principales intermediarios entre la ciencia que se había desarrollado en el mundo árabe y la Europa cristiana

claims.text: לפי המאמר מחיפה, במונחי חשבון מסוימים נהג בר חייא בחוסר עקביות והשתמש במילים שונות למושג מתמטי אחד.

claims.text: לפי קורצה, על פי כתבי היד התרגום הסתיים ב-30 ביוני 1116.
claims.quote: da nach den Handschriften die Übersetzung am 15. Tage des Monats Saphar im Jahre DX der Araber, d. h. am 30. Juni 1116 beendet ist.

claims.text: לפי DSB (פלאטו מטיבולי), החיבור תורגם מעברית ב-1145; כתבי היד נותנים את התאריך הנכון בלוח הנוצרי אך שנת הג'רה שגויה (510/1116 במקום 540/1145).
claims.quote: translated from the Hebrew in 1145 [the manuscripts give the right astronomical equivalent of this date but the wrong Hegira year, 510/1116 instead of 540/1145]

claims.text: לפי המילון הביוגרפי הספרדי, החיבור תורגם ללטינית בידי פלאטו מטיבולי ב-1145 בשם Liber embadorum, ספר האלגברה הערבית העתיק ביותר שנכתב באירופה, ובו ניתן לראשונה פתרון למשוואות ריבועיות.

claims.text: לפי המילון הספרדי, בין המומחים יש ויכוח על מועד מותו, ותאריך 1136 התקבל באופן מסורתי.
claims.quote: En cuanto a la fecha de su muerte hay discusión entre los especialistas. Tradicionalmente se ha aceptado la fecha de 1136

claims.text: לפי המאמר מחיפה, על פי השערות חי בר חייא בין 1065 ל-1136, אך יש הסוברים שעדיין חי ב-1145.

quote_translations.c56: Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi was a Jewish mathematician, astronomer and philosopher who lived and worked in Spain.
quote_translations.c50: Abraham bar Hiyya became famous thanks to his important book written in Hebrew, 'Hibbur ha-Meshihah ve-ha-Tishboret', which appeared in 1116.
quote_translations.c58: This title indicates a high public and legal office that Bar Hiyya held at the royal court of Barcelona.
quote_translations.c63: The book is divided into four parts. The first part contains definitions of basic concepts in geometry and arithmetic and main theorems
quote_translations.c64: The third part deals with the division of areas, and the fourth with the calculation of volumes.
quote_translations.c66: Bar Hiyya accepted only the positive value as a solution, because in his time negative numbers had no meaning.
quote_translations.c65: Bar Hiyya succeeded, clearly and precisely, in describing formulas and presenting diagrams using verbal explanations only.
quote_translations.c67: As we see, Bar Hiyya used the numerical values of the Hebrew letters to denote numbers
quote_translations.c68: He divides the circle into thin strips, straightens them, lays them one on top of another and obtains a triangle
quote_translations.c69: And afterwards multiply half the diameter by half the circumference line, and you will find the area of the circle
quote_translations.c53: The book contains instruction in measurements, and in fact it is the first book in the Western world that contains knowledge of trigonometry and of the theory of measurement that was known to the Arabs.
quote_translations.c51: The book was translated into Latin in 1145 by Plato of Tivoli and for hundreds of years served as a textbook for land surveyors.
quote_translations.c54: Many mathematicians, among them Leonardo Pisano (Fibonacci), were deeply influenced by the book.
quote_translations.c59: The book's originality is expressed in its being the first book written in Hebrew that deals with matters of mathematics and astronomy.
quote_translations.c60: He coined not only individual words, but entire systems of words and of scientific terms
quote_translations.c70: He is the first craftsman who systematically expanded the boundaries of the Hebrew language and gave it a scientific terminology
quote_translations.c61: With regard to some of the arithmetic terms Bar Hiyya was inconsistent; he used different words for a single mathematical concept
quote_translations.c62: Whereas the definition of the diameter of the circle lacks the necessary statement that it passes through the center
quote_translations.c55: According to these conjectures Abraham bar Hiyya lived between the years 1065 and 1136, but some say that he was still alive in 1145.
